skill_drafts.name: Cache Eviction Algorithm Selection
skill_drafts.description: Evaluate and select between FIFO-based and LRU-based cache eviction strategies based on workload characteristics and efficiency requirements. Determines whether queue type materially impacts cache hit ratio and performance.
skill_drafts.objective: Choose optimal cache eviction queue type for given workload
applicable_signals: Multiple eviction algorithm candidates under consideration
Workload traces or access patterns available for testing
contraindications: Cache system is already deployed and locked in production
Workload characteristics are unknown or highly volatile
Performance is not a primary design constraint
Experimental infrastructure or test traces are unavailable
intervention_moves: Implement both FIFO and LRU queue variants
Run experiments on representative workload traces
Measure hit ratio, miss ratio, and efficiency metrics for each variant
Apply quick demotion technique consistently to both implementations
Compare results across diverse workload types (not just single traces)
workflow_steps: {'step': 1, 'action': 'Prepare test environment', 'detail': 'Gather representative workload traces and access patterns; set up benchmarking infrastructure to measure hit ratio, miss ratio, and efficiency metrics.'}
{'step': 2, 'action': 'Implement FIFO variant', 'detail': 'Build cache with FIFO queues (small probationary queue + main queue) and quick demotion on one-hit wonders.'}
{'step': 3, 'action': 'Implement LRU variant', 'detail': 'Build cache with LRU queues replacing both small and main queues; apply same quick demotion logic and hit/eviction-based object movement.'}
{'step': 4, 'action': 'Run comparative experiments', 'detail': 'Execute both implementations on all workload traces; record hit ratio, miss ratio, and efficiency metrics for each.'}
{'step': 5, 'action': 'Analyze results', 'detail': 'Compare efficiency across traces. Check whether LRU consistently outperforms FIFO or whether differences are negligible or trace-specific.'}

{'step': 6, 'action': 'Document decision', 'detail': 'Record selected queue type, rationale (efficiency gain or equivalence), and any workload-specific caveats. Prefer FIFO if efficiency is equivalent (simpler, lower overhead).'}
triggers: Designing or tuning a new cache system
Comparing eviction algorithm candidates for performance optimization
Workload characteristics are known or measurable
Cache efficiency is a primary design constraint
constraints: Test on multiple representative workload traces, not just one or two
Apply quick demotion uniformly to both queue types for fair comparison
Account for edge cases and tail behavior (e.g., adversarial workloads)
Document parameter choices (e.g., queue size ratios, demotion thresholds)
cautions: Parameter tuning for individual traces is easy but does not generalize; validate across diverse workloads
Adaptive algorithms may overreact to small workload perturbations; prefer simpler fixed-parameter designs when efficiency is equivalent
Miss ratio curves for scan-heavy workloads are often non-convex; do not assume gradient-based optimization will find global optimum
output_contract: Selected queue type (FIFO or LRU) with documented rationale. Deliverable includes: (1) comparative efficiency metrics across workload traces, (2) statement of whether LRU provides measurable improvement, (3) recommended queue type and justification, (4) any workload-specific constraints or exceptions.

examples.input: Cache system design for general-purpose workload with mixed access patterns; FIFO and LRU candidates available; hit ratio is primary metric.
examples.output: Select FIFO with quick demotion. Experiments show LRU does not improve hit ratio over FIFO when quick demotion is applied; FIFO is simpler and has lower overhead.
examples.notes: Applies when workload is not adversarial and quick demotion is implemented uniformly.

examples.input: Tuning cache for adversarial workload (e.g., scan-heavy, non-convex miss ratio curve); both FIFO and LRU tested on tail traces.
examples.output: Document that LRU may help on 2% of tail traces but does not generalize; recommend FIFO with fixed queue size (easier to tune than adaptive algorithm).
examples.notes: Highlights that adaptive algorithms are hard to tune across diverse workloads; fixed-parameter FIFO is more robust.

metadata.prompt: Compare FIFO and LRU queue implementations for your cache system. Run experiments with both queue-type combinations on representative workload traces. Measure cache hit ratio, miss ratio, and efficiency metrics. Document whether LRU provides measurable improvement over FIFO with quick demotion applied. Select the simpler option (FIFO) if efficiency is equivalent.

skill_drafts.name: Adaptive Algorithm Parameter Tuning Risk Assessment
skill_drafts.description: Identify and document risks and failure modes when tuning multiple interdependent parameters in adaptive cache algorithms. Assesses whether adaptive tuning is justified given workload predictability, parameter sensitivity, and convexity assumptions.
skill_drafts.objective: Prevent over-tuning, parameter explosion, and overfitting in adaptive cache algorithms
applicable_signals: Presence of multiple coupled parameters (e.g., queue resize frequency, space moved per resize, queue size bounds, trigger thresholds)
Tuning success on subset of traces but failure on others
Small workload perturbations causing large performance swings
Implicit convexity assumption in algorithm design
contraindications: Workload is stable and well-characterized across representative traces
Adaptive algorithm has been validated on comprehensive trace suite
Parameter space is small and well-understood
Fixed-parameter baseline already meets performance requirements
workflow_steps: {'step': 1, 'action': 'Enumerate all tunable parameters', 'detail': 'List each parameter, its range, and dependencies on other parameters (e.g., ARC ghost queue hit handling, queue resize frequency and amount)'}
{'step': 2, 'action': 'Assess tuning generalization', 'detail': 'Test whether parameters tuned on a subset of traces perform well on held-out traces; document failure rate and performance variance'}

{'step': 3, 'action': 'Validate algorithm assumptions', 'detail': 'Check whether miss-ratio curves are convex for your workload class; identify workload types (e.g., scan-heavy) where assumptions break'}
{'step': 4, 'action': 'Measure perturbation sensitivity', 'detail': 'Introduce small workload variations and measure performance impact; flag if algorithm overreacts'}

{'step': 5, 'action': 'Document risk and recommendation', 'detail': 'Summarize parameter coupling, tuning brittleness, and convexity violations; recommend fixed-parameter design, downsized simulation-based tuning, or simpler algorithm'}
triggers: Evaluating an adaptive cache algorithm with multiple tunable parameters
Workload is adversarial, non-stationary, or poorly characterized
Past performance traces may not predict future behavior
Parameter tuning has been attempted on limited trace sets
constraints: Assessment must document all tunable parameters and their interdependencies
Must evaluate generalization risk: tuning on subset vs. full trace set
Must check whether miss-ratio curve assumptions hold for workload class
Must quantify sensitivity to workload perturbations
cautions: Parameter tuning that works on a few traces often fails to generalize
Adaptive algorithms may overreact to small workload changes without explicit balancing mechanisms
Convexity assumptions may not hold for scan-heavy or streaming workloads
Adding more parameters to 'fix' tuning brittleness increases complexity without solving root cause
output_contract: Risk assessment document containing: (1) parameter inventory with coupling analysis, (2) generalization test results and failure modes, (3) convexity validation for workload class, (4) perturbation sensitivity measurements, (5) explicit recommendation (accept adaptive algorithm with caveats, use fixed parameters, use simulation-based tuning, or switch to simpler algorithm)

examples.input: Adaptive cache algorithm with 4 tunable parameters (queue resize frequency, space moved per resize, queue size lower bound, resize trigger threshold); tuning performed on 3 representative traces
examples.output: Risk assessment identifies parameter coupling (resize frequency and space moved are interdependent), generalization failure on 2 of 10 held-out traces, and convexity violation on scan-heavy workloads. Recommendation: use fixed parameters derived from simulation-based tuning on full trace set, or switch to S3-FIFO (FIFO-only, no promotion, minimal tuning)
examples.notes: Based on ARC and S3-FIFO-d comparison in source

examples.input: Workload is stable and well-characterized; adaptive algorithm has been validated on 50+ representative traces with consistent performance
examples.output: Assessment concludes adaptive algorithm is justified; no risk flag. Proceed with deployment.
examples.notes: Contraindication case: assessment returns low risk

metadata.prompt: Before committing to an adaptive algorithm with multiple tunable parameters, evaluate: (1) How many parameters require tuning and how are they coupled? (2) Does tuning on sample traces generalize to unseen workloads? (3) Does the algorithm assume convex miss-ratio curves, and is this assumption valid for your workload class? (4) How sensitive is performance to small workload perturbations? If brittleness is high, recommend fixed-parameter design or downsized simulation-based tuning instead.

skill_drafts.name: One-Hit Wonder Eviction Policy
skill_drafts.description: Quickly demote and remove single-access cache items (one-hit wonders) from the main cache queue before they can pollute the working set. This micro-skill targets transient or scan-like requests that would otherwise occupy cache space without contributing to future hits.
skill_drafts.objective: Remove low-reuse items from cache quickly to improve hit ratio on scan-heavy workloads
applicable_signals: Workload contains high proportion of non-repeating requests
Cache hit ratio degradation due to one-time accesses
contraindications: All items in workload expected to have high reuse
Cache size is very small relative to working set
Demotion latency is critical to system performance
Workload is uniform and does not contain scan patterns
workflow_steps: {'step': 1, 'action': 'Monitor cache item access count upon each access'}
{'step': 2, 'action': 'On first access, place item in probationary queue or mark with one-hit flag'}
{'step': 3, 'action': 'On second access, promote item to main FIFO queue if it shows reuse'}
{'step': 4, 'action': 'If item is not accessed again within probationary window, evict it'}
{'step': 5, 'action': 'Track probationary queue occupancy and adjust demotion aggressiveness if needed'}
triggers: Cache item receives exactly one access
Scan, streaming, or sequential access pattern detected in workload
constraints: Probationary queue must be pre-allocated and sized appropriately
Demotion decision must be made before item ages further in main queue
One-hit items must not be promoted back to main queue on subsequent access without explicit policy
cautions: Overly aggressive demotion may evict items that would have been reused
Probationary queue size must be tuned; too small causes thrashing, too large wastes space
Policy assumes miss ratio curve behavior; may not work optimally on non-convex workloads
output_contract: One-hit items successfully removed from main cache queue before polluting working set. Probationary queue size reduced. Cache hit ratio improved on scan-heavy traces. Observable metric: reduction in cache misses caused by transient requests.

examples.input: Cache workload with 30% scan requests; item X accessed once, then never again
examples.output: Item X placed in probationary queue, evicted after time window expires; main cache space freed for reusable items
examples.notes: Typical scan-heavy scenario where one-hit wonders degrade hit ratio

examples.input: Sequential streaming access pattern; 100 items accessed once each
examples.output: All 100 items moved to probationary queue; evicted in FIFO order; main cache preserved for working set

metadata.prompt: Identify cache items that have been accessed exactly once. Move them from the main FIFO queue to a probationary queue or mark them for immediate eviction. Ensure the demotion happens before the item can be promoted or aged further in the main cache. Monitor probationary queue occupancy and evict items that do not show repeated access within a defined time window.
